deep.reconstruction:
Context: the previous page expands Kepler's equation E = M + e f(E), with f = sin, as a Lagrange series and computes dE/dM. This page states the general rule behind that, the reversion of a power series, with the coefficients written as Laurent coefficients.

Setup:
(1) y = X(x) = αx + βx^2 + γx^3 + ..., with α ≠ 0.
(2) For each n ≥ 1, expand X^{-n} as a Laurent series starting at x^{-n}. Gauss uses primes (upper indices) to label which power n is meant:
- 1/X = a'/x + b' + c'x + d'x^2 + ...
- 1/X^2 = a''/x^2 + b''/x + c'' + d''x + ...
- 1/X^3 = a'''/x^3 + b'''/x^2 + c'''/x + d''' + ...
- and so on.
So the letter a, b, c, d, ... is the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, ... coefficient of X^{-n}, i.e. the coefficient of x^{-n}, x^{-n+1}, x^{-n+2}, ...

Claimed inversion formulas:
- x = a' y + (1/2) b'' y^2 + (1/3) c''' y^3 + ...
- x^2 = a'' y^2 + (2/3) b''' y^3 + (2/4) c'''' y^4 + ...
- x^3 = a''' y^3 + (3/4) b'''' y^4 + (3/5) c^v y^5 + ...

General rule (my formulation): [y^n] x^k = (k/n) · [x^{-k}] X(x)^{-n}, i.e. (k/n) times the residue of x^{k-1} X^{-n}.
- In Gauss's labelling, the coefficient of x^{-k} in X^{-n} is the (n−k+1)-th letter with n primes.
- For k = 1 it is the coefficient of 1/x: a', b'', c''', ...
- For k = 2 it is the coefficient of x^{-2}: a'', b''', c'''', ...
- For k = 3 it is the coefficient of x^{-3}: a''', b'''', c^v, ...

Why it holds (my addition, not on the page): write y = X(x) and take the residue at y = 0 of x^k / y^{n+1}. Substituting y = X(x) and integrating by parts gives (k/n) res_x x^{k-1} X^{-n}.

Purpose: to have a general rule for reverting the series in the Kepler-equation work on the previous page. The next page turns to orbit computation for the comet of 1772/1805.
errors: Line 2 has an exponent slip: it reads 1/X = a'/x + b' + c'xx + d'x^3 ... but should read c'x + d'x^2 + ..., to match the pattern of the 1/X^2 and 1/X^3 lines. The slip is harmless, since only a' is used afterwards.
All three inversion formulas are correct as stated.

results.what: Coefficients of the reversed series x(y), and of its powers x^k, expressed through Laurent coefficients of X^{-n}: [y^n] x^k = (k/n) [x^{-k}] X^{-n}
results.modern_name: Lagrange inversion theorem (Lagrange–Bürmann), in its residue / coefficient-extraction form
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1770) and Bürmann (1799) for the inversion series; the residue formulation is usually attributed to Cauchy and Jacobi (Jacobi 1830, 'De resolutione aequationum per series infinitas')

deep.surprise_reason: Lagrange inversion itself was well known by 1805, and Gauss used it for Kepler's equation. However, stating it cleanly as (k/n) times the coefficient of x^{-k} in X^{-n}, covering all powers x^k, anticipates the residue form usually associated with Jacobi (1830). It is a notable unpublished detail, but not a new theorem.
